**Code.** Branch `phase1/planar` of `Symplectomorphism/c-gnn`, commit
`d810e32`. New: `marking/edits.py`,
`physics/planar_hold.py`, `tests/test_planar_step2.py` (17 tests); changed:
`Cand`, the solver's success check and the search's acceptance, for planar
scenes only. Angelo's 3D path is untouched.

::: {.callout-important title="Updated for Decision 9 (Nov 7, 2026): Xiao and Ji's construction"}
Commit `9261ece` replaces three parts of this step with Xiao and Ji's
construction ([Decision 9](xiao-ji.qmd)):

- **Exclusions within a pair are derived:** one contact per convex element
  pair, none alongside a contact it contains.
- **Transfers are Xiao–Ji containment only:** 56 pairs, down from 92. The
  disk now goes round a box corner in two transfers.
- **Pass-through becomes the general compound rule:** all changes relaxing
  or all constraining, kept only if every proper subset is invalid.

The gate tests statics of the less-constrained end of each edit. The landed
box is {t}, so landing is the transfer s<sub>v</sub> → t. Superseded text
below is marked.
:::

## What step 2 changes

Step 1 made the contact labels right. Step 2 makes the planner's menu of
edits right. `Cand` proposes an edit only when it passes the paper's
checks:

- **The edit is an edge of the marking graph:** both the current formation
  and the new one are **Valid**. No two excluded contacts ({g, t}, {g<sub>v</sub>, s},
  {g, s<sub>v</sub>}, {g, m<sub>z</sub>}), at most one contact per convex
  element pair, and no contact alongside one it contains (per body pair
  before Decision 9).
- **Near:** a contact it adds is already within the gap gate.
- **H:** the contacts that persist through the edit hold the box at the
  current pose.

The menu now has five kinds of edit:

| Edit | Changes | Example |
|---|---|---|
| make(c), break(c) | one contact | make(s): push the box against the riser |
| transport | nothing (moves the pose) | slide the box along the floor |
| **transfer(c → d)** (new) | one contact for one it contains, or the reverse (Xiao–Ji cases 2–3) | g → g<sub>v</sub>: the box starts to tip onto its corner; s<sub>v</sub> → t: it lands |
| **compound** (new; "pass-through" before Decision 9) | several single changes that cannot be separated | the pivot: g → g<sub>v</sub> and s → s<sub>v</sub> at once |

Transport is now offered only when the current formation is supported,
as the paper defines it; before, it was always legal.

**At the start** ({g}, box flat on the floor), `Cand` no longer offers a
second floor contact, t, s<sub>v</sub> or m<sub>z</sub> (all excluded with g), or the
transfer g → g<sub>v</sub>. That last one is refused by H: during the swap only
the box's corner would still touch the floor, and one corner cannot hold a
flat box.

## Pass-through, made precise

::: {.callout-warning title="Superseded by Decision 9 (Nov 7, 2026)"}
The two-transfer rule below is replaced by Xiao and Ji's neighbor relation.
An edge applies a set of single changes (make, break, transfer), all
relaxing or all constraining. It is kept only if the result is valid and
every nonempty proper subset of the changes gives an invalid formation;
compound edges are capped at three changes.

On the step this gives the same compound edges, the pivot and its reverse
(128 instances), and searching up to four changes finds no more. A make
followed by a break in one pair is still not an edit, because it passes
through a valid formation. The rest of this section is kept as the record
of choice 1.
:::

Decision 7 adopted pass-through edges for the pivot: from {m<sub>x</sub>, g, s}
the box can only reach {m<sub>x</sub>, g<sub>v</sub>, s<sub>v</sub>} by changing two contacts at
once, because both one-at-a-time intermediates, {g<sub>v</sub>, s} and
{g, s<sub>v</sub>}, are excluded. Taken literally ("some sequence of steps
through invalid markings"), the definition would also let any contact
replace any other contact of its pair in one edit: make the new one first,
which is invalid because the pair then has two, then break the old one.
That would make transfer adjacency pointless.

**Implemented:** two single steps in different body pairs whose
intermediates are invalid *in both orders*. Both must then be transfers
with crossed exclusions. On the step scene the only pass-throughs are the
pivot and its reverse. A brute-force search over all 12,393 markings with
at most one contact per pair finds exactly the same 128 pass-through edges.

::: {.callout-note title="Settled (Nov 7, 2026): the two-transfer rule"}
Let w → x be a transfer in one body pair and y → z a transfer in another,
with x excluded alongside y and w excluded alongside z (while w with y,
and x with z, are allowed). Then **pass(w → x, y → z)** replaces w and y by
x and z in one edit. It is an edge when both ends are valid markings.
It is the **only** edit that changes more than one body pair:

- A make followed by a break in the *same* pair is not an edit. The
  in-between state has two contacts in one pair, which is not a marking,
  and allowing it would let any contact replace any other, skipping
  transfer adjacency.
- A move that needs three or more inseparable steps is not an edge. A
  scene that needs one gets it as a new generator by its own decision.
- A transfer paired with a make or a break never qualifies: two single
  edits whose in-between states are both invalid are always two such
  transfers.

The literal "any sequence through invalid markings" rule, restricted to
one contact per pair, finds the same edges on this scene but needs a
search instead of a closed form, so it was declined.
:::

## H: persistent contacts, decided exactly {#h-exact}

::: {.callout-note title="Since Decision 9: statics of the less-constrained end"}
Every edge now links a formation to one it contains, so H tests the
**less-constrained end**: the new formation for a relaxing edit, the
current one for a constraining edit. This is the transition rule of
multi-contact planning. Hauser et al. (2008): the robot "can support itself
only with forces applied at the contact in [σ]", since "the applied force
is zero at the instant of time when the contact is made or broken".
Hauser, Bretl and Latombe (2005) and Escande et al. (2013) state the same
rule.

The test suite checks that the less-constrained end equals the persisting
contacts below, for make, break, both transfer directions and the pivot.
The old contact's normal (choice 2) now follows from containment: the
feature that defines the normal is the one that stays.
:::

H asks whether the contacts that **persist** through the edit hold the box
(Decision 7). For a make or a break that is the paper's rule (the contacts
kept). For a transfer, only the part of the old contact set that the new
one still covers persists: for g → g<sub>v</sub>, the box's corner.

::: {.callout-note title="Settled (Nov 7, 2026): the old contact's normal"}
The forces on those persisting points use the **old** contact's normal (and
friction, which is the same for every contact of a body pair). H is checked
at the current pose, where the old marking is realized and the new one is
not, so the old contact's geometry is what carries the load. On the demo
trajectory (1,155 transfer edits), the two normals differ by at most 1.77°
where the new contact is about to be realized (within the on-set angle
1.83°). They differ by up to 179° only where the new contact is far from
realized, and there its normal is not a real force. Using the new normal
changes none of the 1,155 decisions.
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**Background tutorial:** [Deciding support exactly](bg-exact-hold-test.qmd)
derives this test step by step, with a worked example, proofs of the witness,
certificate and margin, and exercises.
[The hold test as a linear program](bg-hold-lp.qmd) poses the same question
as LPs that also serve the 3D build. Since Nov 7 that backbone is the
default gate ([below](#gate)); the exact test described next is its
cross-check.
:::

**The test.** In the plane, every contact force is a nonnegative mix of the
two edges of its friction cone. So "the contacts hold the box" means that
the wrench cancelling gravity (x force, z force, moment) lies in a cone in
3D generated by at most 16 vectors. That is decided exactly, with proof
either way:

- **Supported:** a nonnegative combination of at most three generators that
  reproduces the wrench, by Carathéodory's theorem. This is the witness.
- **Not supported:** a plane through the origin with every generator on one
  side and the gravity wrench on the other, by Farkas's lemma. This is the
  certificate. Every face of the cone is spanned by two generators, so the
  candidate planes are few.
- **Margin:** the signed distance from the gravity wrench to the cone's
  boundary, with forces in units of mg and moments in mg·a/2. Inside the
  cone it is the largest disturbance the contacts absorb in every direction;
  outside, minus the distance to the cone. A flat box on the
  floor: 0.196, which is μ/√(1+μ²) for μ = 0.2. With the disk in the
  formation the cone often fills all of 3D, because the disk's force is
  unbounded. A finite margin there needs the manipulator's force limits.
  *Both points are settled since Nov 7: see [the gate](#gate).*

The same function takes a lower friction coefficient and mass and
center-of-mass vertices, and returns the worst-case margin (the robust
margin of Decision 6).

## The pivot needs the disk low

![Whether the box, tipped by θ onto the step corner, holds on the corner and the disk alone ({m<sub>x</sub>, s<sub>v</sub>}): the hold test of break(g<sub>v</sub>), by the default gate (the LP with the disk's motor limits, ±1 N; ℓ₁ margin). Blue: held, with the margin; red: not held, by how much; the black line is the boundary. Blank: the box is not in the formation at that pose. With unlimited disk force the held region was more than twice as large (815 against 382 of the 1,599 poses); everything held here is also held there.](media/step2_pivot_margin.svg){.lightbox}

The chain's canonical pose for σ<sub>3</sub> puts the disk at the middle of
−x<sub>B</sub>. There, H refuses break(g<sub>v</sub>): pushing at mid-height, the disk
cannot keep the box on the step corner without the floor. It must push low
(toward the floor), and, since its motors give at most 1 N per axis, the
box must already be tipped about 40° or more: at 30° holding the box on the
corner takes more force than the motors give, wherever the disk pushes.
Between about 65° and 70° any disk height works; past about 72° the box falls onto the platform. A search gets there by
transport, tilting the box further and moving the disk down the face
within the formation. A float64 LP with the same motor limits confirms
every answer, so this is a fact about the physics (and the motors), not
about the test. The same holds for the landing at σ<sub>4</sub>, now transfer(s<sub>v</sub> → t).

With that, `Cand` offers every step of the chain from a pose in its
formation: make(m<sub>x</sub>), make(s), the pivot (compound),
break(g<sub>v</sub>), transfer(s<sub>v</sub> → t), break(m<sub>x</sub>),
make(m<sub>z</sub>), then transport. *Before Decision 9 the landing was
make(t) and the last edit break(s<sub>v</sub>); the landed box is now {t}.*
Theorem `relocate` holds: with σ = {m<sub>x</sub>, s}, break(m<sub>x</sub>)
is never offered.

## Which hold solver {#which-solver}

The plan was to build H on MPAX, Angelo's LP solver, then benchmark and
switch if a solver won clearly. One did. The benchmark covers 1,000 random
cases and 416 cases within 2 mm of the support boundary. Every answer is
checked against a float64 LP (SciPy's HiGHS) on an independently coded
formulation.

| Backend | Random (1,000) | Near the boundary (416) | ms per 256, CPU / GPU |
|---|---|---|---|
| Old 6-row MPAX LP | 998 | 220 (194 false rejections) | 3,879 / 313 |
| 3-row MPAX LP | 999 | 222 (192 false rejections) | 63 / 110 |
| **Exact, certified** | **1,000** | **393** on CPU, 389 on GPU (21–26 false rejections, 1–2 false acceptances) | **4.3 / 2.0** |

Every error of the exact test lies within 0.33 mm (of disk height) of the
boundary on CPU, and within 0.67 mm on GPU, where float32 geometry decides.
Everywhere 0.7 mm or more away it is right, on both. One GPU pitfall was
caught on the way: JAX runs float32 matrix products on the GPU in reduced
precision (TF32), which broke the test's check of supporting planes; it now
forms every dot product elementwise. The step-1 contact layer is not
affected: on 5,721 poses its gaps agree between CPU and GPU to 2.7 µm, and
its on-sets exactly. Both LPs reject supported formations across the whole 2 mm band:
their "not supported" often meant "ran out of iterations". The exact test
became the hold gate for planar scenes; the MPAX version stays in the code
for comparison. *Since Nov 7 the gate is the LP backbone with actuator
limits, which the exact test cannot take ([the gate](#gate)).*

## The gate since Nov 7: LP, motor limits, ℓ₁ margin {#gate}

::: {.callout-note title="Settled (Nov 7, 2026): step-2 choices 3 and 4"}
**What the margin is.** At the current pose, with the contacts that persist
through the edit: how large a disturbance (a push or twist, in units of mg
and mg·a/2) the contacts can absorb before they can no longer hold the box.
Negative: how far from holding. H uses its sign; Decision 6 uses its value
(to rank formations, as the controller's terminal sets, and checkpoint 5
tests whether it predicts the solver's success).

**Shape: set inclusion.** The margin is the largest r such that the
gravity-cancelling wrench plus r·D is still supported, for a disturbance
polytope D (D is absorbed iff r ≥ 1). By default D is the ℓ₁ unit ball
(pushes and twists along the axes), which makes the margin the signed ℓ₁
distance to the boundary: 0.2 = μ on the flat box. A scene can pass its own
D. The exact test's Euclidean margin is always within a factor √3 of it (√6
in 3D) and stays as a cross-check.

**The disk's force: the simulator's motor limits.** The disk is held by two
slide motors, ±1 N each (`step.xml`). Held still, the motors must supply its
force on the box plus its own weight (0.20 N), so its force on the box is
bounded: two rows per motor in the LP, read from the MuJoCo model. The box
weighs 0.98 N, so **the disk alone cannot hold it up**, and margins with the
disk are finite (no more cap). OpenArm's limits replace these when it
arrives.

**The gate: the LP backbone.** With force limits the set of supportable
wrenches is a polytope, not a cone, and the exact test (which needs a cone)
cannot decide it. So `PlanarHold` and `Cand` now default to `method="lp"`
with the motor limits; `method="exact"` stays as the cone-only cross-check
and MPAX only for comparison.
:::

Checked against a float64 LP (SciPy's HiGHS) that applies the same motor
limits, coded independently (the limits hard-coded from `step.xml`, not
read from the model). Near the boundary means 16 sweeps of disk height on
the pivot, bisected to the boundary, with 13 cases within 2 mm each.

| Gate (float32) | Random (1,000) | Near the boundary | ms per 256, CPU / GPU |
|---|---|---|---|
| **LP + motor limits (default)** | **1,000** | **199 / 202 of 208** (CPU / GPU): no false rejection, no "uncertain" | **14.7 / 3.4** |
| LP, no limits (vs HiGHS without limits) | 1,000 | 386 / 383 of 416 | 8.5 / 2.5 |
| Exact test, no limits (vs HiGHS without limits) | 1,000 | 390 / 389 of 416 | 5.0 / 1.6 |

Every miss of the default gate (9 on CPU, 6 on GPU) is the bisected
boundary pose itself, within 10<sup>−10</sup> m of disk height: the gate's
margin there is 0 (at most 2·10<sup>−7</sup>), and HiGHS in float64 says
"just not". At every offset of 0.33 mm or more, the two agree. With the
limits, no margin reaches the cap (0 of 568 supported cases); without them,
about 190 of 636 did.

## ε<sub>pen</sub> and ties {#eps-pen}

Step 1 left a known issue: with ε<sub>pen</sub> = 10 mm, two contacts of one pair
can both count as touching under deep penetration. Step 2 was to set
ε<sub>pen</sub> from the penetration measured in the solver's rollouts. The
measurement says not yet:

- In 24 full MPPI rollouts of the chain's edits, the pushing edits
  penetrate up to 9.9 mm (95th percentiles 4–8 mm); the passive breaks stay
  under 1.6 mm.
- The cause is MPPI's cost, whose arrival term rewards penetration (the
  shove on walkthrough page 7). A tighter ε<sub>pen</sub> now would fail every
  pushing rollout.
- So ε<sub>pen</sub> moves to step 3, after the cost.

Done now: a pose with a tie can neither count as a solver success nor
become a search node. A stress test in the suite tracks ties on 4,000
jittered demo poses: 357 when step 2 was built, 475 since Decision 9. 474
of the 475 have a contact deeper than ε<sub>on</sub>, and in 136 of them
s<sub>v</sub> loses to t, which contains it. The test's budget is 500.

One more finding for step 3: all 24 rollouts fail the solver's success
check, the passive breaks included, and not because of ties.

## Checks

- **The marking graph, exhaustively** (11,959 valid markings; since
  Decision 9, 37,203 of the 59,049 markings with at most one contact per
  convex element pair):
  - every edge lands on a valid formation;
  - every edge has its reverse;
  - the degree bound holds;
  - the graph is connected, and its distance is between a quarter of the
    Hamming distance and the Hamming distance.

  These are the claims of the restated Lemma `markgraph-struct` in the
  paper.
- **Supported against the float64 LP:** 250 random cases and the pivot
  scan, all certified, all equal.
- **The cone test** against HiGHS on 400 random cones in 3D, plus the
  degenerate cases (wedge, ray, empty, all of 3D).
- **The full suite**, 48 tests, passes on Python 3.14 (CPU and GPU) and 3.12.
  Since Decision 9: 68 tests on Python 3.14, CPU and GPU.
